title: The Workplace Broke Gen Z and Then Blamed Them for It
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that senior leaders who call Gen Z fragile, entitled or uncommitted are misreading evidence and misdiagnosing structural conditions as character flaws. He cites the Mental Health UK Burnout Report 2025, in which 18 to 24 year olds are most at risk and comfort discussing stress with a manager fell from 75 percent to 56 percent in a year, and a Deloitte survey showing 40 percent of Gen Z feel stressed most or all of the time. He sets this against the economic reality these workers inherited, including insecure housing, stagnant entry wages, zero-hours contracts and automation anxiety, and says the old psychological contract of loyalty for security has been broken too often to trust. He adds a commercial argument that organisations dismissing flexibility and mental health expectations lose access to talent. The sharpest move is turning the criticism back on leaders: judging Gen Z against a template formed in a different labour market is a failure of contextual analysis. He closes by asking leaders what they are asking young staff to get on with, and whether that question survives scrutiny.
points: Survey data from Mental Health UK and Deloitte point to high burnout and stress among young workers, and to a sharp fall in willingness to discuss stress with line managers.
The generational complaint ignores structural conditions such as housing costs, student debt, stagnant entry wages and a labour market being reshaped by AI.
Treating wellbeing and flexibility expectations as unreasonable carries a commercial cost, because employers that adapt gain retention, lower absenteeism and a larger talent pool.
Leaders who judge Gen Z by their own early-career conditions commit a failure of contextual analysis, which the author calls a core leadership competency.
His closing test for leaders is to ask what they are telling young staff to get on with and whether that demand survives honest scrutiny.
quotes: The proportion of young workers who feel comfortable discussing stress with their line manager fell from 75% in the 2024 Burnout Report to 56% in 2025. This is a collapse, in a single year, that should alarm anyone who believes manager relationships are the foundation of good mental health at work.
Deloitte’s 2024 Gen Z and Millennial Survey, drawing on responses from over 22,000 people across 44 countries, found that 40% of Gen Z respondents feel stressed most or all of the time.

They came of age watching institutions (governments, banks, employers) fail at scale. They face housing costs that would make their managers’ first purchases unrecognisable. They carry student debt that previous generations did not.

The psychological contract (work hard, demonstrate loyalty, be rewarded with security and progression) has been demonstrably broken enough times that trusting it requires a leap of faith that the evidence does not support.

Framing Gen Z’s workplace behaviour as a generational character deficiency is both inaccurate and commercially costly. The organisations that treat younger workers’ expectations around flexibility, mental health support, and meaningful work as unreasonable demands are systematically losing access to a significant proportion of the available talent pool.

The people most likely to characterise Gen Z as difficult are often those whose own early career was shaped by very different structural conditions: lower housing costs, more stable employment contracts, a clearer relationship between effort and reward, and a labour market not yet reshaped by AI.

Their template for what ‘normal’ working life looks like does not map onto the world their younger colleagues inhabit. That is a failure of contextual analysis; and contextual analysis is supposed to be a core competency of leadership.
As a result, the question we need to ask is ‘What are we asking them to get on with, and does that question survive scrutiny?’ Most of the time, if you ask it honestly, it does not.
